_read_me: The rules both checks run on. Two kinds, kept apart on purpose.
1. tokenHashes - the names that must never appear here or in the published
tarball. They are stored as SALTED HASHES, never as text. The previous
version of this file listed them in the clear, captioned with what each
one was, in a PUBLIC repository - a denylist of secrets is a list of
secrets, and it was also the one file the sweep skipped, so the sweep
structurally could not see it. Nothing is skipped now, because nothing
sensitive is written down.
Honesty about what this does and does not buy: sha256 over a short,
guessable name is not secrecy. A reader who already knows a name can
confirm it. What this removes is the PUBLICATION - the list, the
captions, and the shape of the platform, handed to a stranger.
2. patterns - generic shapes that give nothing away (SQL keywords, a source
map marker, a run of nineteen digits). Their `regex` is base64 so that
this file is not a match for itself; that is a self-reference fix, NOT
secrecy, and they decode to exactly what their label says.
`npm run rules:show` prints the decoded patterns and the hash count.
What the hashes do NOT do, said here rather than discovered later: they are
a confirmation oracle. With a wordlist assembled from this project's own
README, a reviewer recovered most of them in seconds. That is accepted, not
overlooked - this is internal naming with no access value and nothing to
rotate. The gain was never the strings; it was losing the captions that said
what each name was, and losing the exemption that stopped the sweep from
reading the one file that mattered.
Keeping this file in the public repository is also a decision: behind a
secret, neither check could run for an outside contributor or in a fork, so
it would report success in exactly the case it exists for.
_tokenLength: The shortest and longest entry behind the hashes, in characters.
The decoders size themselves from the shortest: a threshold chosen without
reference to what is being looked for is how a check comes to report success
about what it never read. The first version demanded 18 bytes of plaintext
before it would look at base64, and no entry was that long.
A length range is a disclosure, so it is kept as small as it can be: the one
class whose space a length hint collapses is not on this list any more (see
_numbers). What remains is long enough that a length bound adds nothing a
wordlist did not already give, which is the limitation _read_me concedes.
blindSpots() derives its statement from these numbers, so it cannot claim a
coverage the thresholds do not give.
_tokenHashes: sha256(`${salt}:${token.toLowerCase()}`). A finding reports the hash prefix
and the file and line - never the token, because a CI log on a public
repository is as public as this file.
_allowedHosts: The public repository may name these and nothing else. apache.org is the
licence, github.com is this repository, viafrei.de and mcp.viafrei.de are
the public service. The loopback and the reserved .invalid TLD belong to

_samples: Each tarball/embedded-source pattern carries a `sample`: a base64 string
that the pattern must match. The gate's self-test poisons a copy of the
real tarball with it, so a rule added here is a case added there and the
self-test never has to spell a forbidden string out itself. The repository
patterns carry no sample - one of them is a run of nineteen digits, and a
sample of that is the very thing this repository may not contain.
_numbers: Numbers are NOT hashed, and this is the round-3 defect being repaired.
A hash of a value drawn from a small enumerable space is not a hash, it is
the value with extra steps: a reviewer exhausted the space of one such class
in 49 milliseconds on a laptop, with the salt taken from this file and no
wordlist at all. Publishing a minimum length made it worse.
So that class is not on the hash list any more. It is covered instead by the
opposite construction: an ALLOW-list of the numbers this repository may
contain, with no captions. An allow-list gives a reader nothing - these are
the numbers that are here, which they can already see - and it is strictly
stronger than the hashes were, because it catches every internal value of
this shape, including the ones nobody thought to add.
Adding one: if a number in this range is genuinely part of this repository,
put it here. If it is an internal value, it does not belong in the file at
all, and the point of the check is that you have to make that choice.
_patterns: Each pattern is stored base64-encoded AND reversed, and both halves of that
are load-bearing. base64 keeps the file from matching its own rules when it
is read as text; reversing keeps it from matching them when it is read as
base64, which the scanner now also does. Neither is secrecy - the shapes are
generic and `npm run rules:show` prints them - it is a file that must not be
a hit for itself while still being scanned like every other file.
